name: The Portuguese reach the coast

summary.text: The first Europeans to reach the coast of what is now Nigeria were Portuguese sailors. Rui de Sequeira sailed into the Bight of Benin in 1472 and named the lagoon at Eko Lago de Curamo, from which Lagos takes its name. In about 1485 João Afonso de Aveiro came up the creeks to Ughoton, Benin's port, and on to Benin City. Benin and Portugal built a strong trade: the Edo sold ivory, pepper, palm oil and captives for manillas and guns, and in the early 16th century the Oba sent an ambassador to Lisbon while Portugal sent missionaries to Benin City.
summary.note: It is not certain how far the 1472 voyage went; Aveiro's visit of about 1485 (or 1486) is the first documented Portuguese visit to Benin.

moments.title: Lago de Curamo
moments.text: Rui de Sequeira sails into the Bight of Benin and names the lagoon around Eko Lago de Curamo. The name Lagos is Portuguese for lakes.

moments.title: Portuguese ships at Ughoton
moments.text: João Afonso de Aveiro reaches Ughoton, the port of Benin, and goes on to the Oba's court: the first documented Portuguese visit to Benin.

moments.title: Trade with Benin
moments.text: The Edo trade ivory, pepper, palm oil and captives for European manillas and guns. Some people in Benin City still spoke a pidgin Portuguese in the late 19th century.

moments.title: An ambassador to Lisbon
moments.text: The Oba sends an ambassador to Lisbon, and the king of Portugal sends Christian missionaries to Benin City.

reviewNotes: Sea lanes are drawn, not traced: the ships come in from the west, along the coast from the Portuguese fort at Elmina, but the exact courses are not recorded.
Ryder (1969) is the standard history of Benin and the Portuguese; the dates here come from the web sources and should be checked against it.
